extracted.intended_audience: registered patent practitioners (patent attorneys/agents) before the USPTO, OED/disciplinary staff, Administrative Law Judges, and respondents in PTO disciplinary proceedings
extracted.subtask_description: Standards, procedural rules, and sanctioning criteria applied in USPTO disciplinary proceedings (service, pleading deadlines, default, professional-conduct rules, and factors for imposing sanctions). Useful for understanding obligations of registered practitioners and the procedures/relief available in OED disciplinary matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Service of complaint (37 C.F.R. § 11.35(a)(2))
rubrics_metrics.description: The Director may serve a complaint on a respondent "[b]y mailing a copy of the complaint by 'Express Mail,' first-class mail, or any delivery service that provides ability to confirm delivery or attempted delivery to ... [a] respondent who is a registered practitioner at the address provided to OED pursuant to § 11.11," or to a non-registered respondent's last known address.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Service is accomplished when the Complaint is mailed and delivered by first-class mail, return receipt requested, to the address provided to the Director pursuant to Rule 11.11; service does not require that the respondent personally take delivery. Evidence of USPS tracking and return receipts may prove compliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practitioner duty to notify change of contact information (37 C.F.R. § 11.11(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: An attorney or agent registered to appear before the PTO must notify the Director in writing of his or her postal address for office, e-mail addresses, and business telephone number, as well as every change to any of said addresses or telephone numbers within thirty days of the date of the change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to notify the Director of changes (e.g., new office address) may result in communications being returned and in practitioner discipline if it causes failures to receive PTO correspondence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Computation of time (37 C.F.R. § 1.7)
rubrics_metrics.description: Deadlines are computed according to the rules for computation of time in patent cases; e.g., an Answer due 30 days after filing, with the due date falling on the first business day that is not a Saturday, Sunday, or Federal holiday.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners must account for weekends and federal holidays when calculating filing deadlines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure to file a timely Answer yields default/admission (37 C.F.R. § 11.36(e))
rubrics_metrics.description: Respondent's failure to file a timely Answer to a Complaint constitutes an admission of the allegations in the Complaint and permits entry of a default judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where a respondent has not answered or otherwise appeared, the hearing officer need not allow time for a response to a motion for default; default may be entered and allegations accepted as true.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedure for motions for default when respondent hasn't appeared
rubrics_metrics.description: In the context of a motion for default, where the respondent has not answered the complaint or otherwise appeared in the proceeding, it is not necessary to allow time for a response to the motion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited precedent (Bovard v. Uland) supports denying response time for default motions if respondent failed to appear; motions can be decided on the record of service and non-response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty of competence / neglect (Rule 10.77(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must act competently; neglect of legal matters entrusted to them violates Rule 10.77(c).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Neglecting client matters (failing to respond to PTO actions, allowing applications to become abandoned) is a serious violation of competence obligations and can support exclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to inform clients of significant PTO correspondence (Rules 10.23(a),(b) via 10.23(c)(5))
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must inform clients of correspondences received from the PTO that could have significant effects on matters pending before the PTO, were received by the respondent on behalf of the clients, and are correspondences of which a reasonable practitioner would believe the clients should be notified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failing to notify clients of Office Actions, Notices of Abandonment, Notices of Allowance, or other impactful PTO correspondence constitutes disreputable or gross misconduct under these rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to advise Director of suspension of state license (Rules 10.23(c)(14) and Rule 11.6)
rubrics_metrics.description: A registered practitioner must advise the Director in writing if his or her license to practice law in a state has been suspended; failing to do so is disreputable or gross misconduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Knowingly failing to notify the Director that a state license has been suspended may independently violate the disciplinary rules and support discipline or exclusion from PTO practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obligation to represent clients zealously within law (Rule 10.84(a)(1))
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must represent their clients zealously and seek the lawful objectives of their clients through reasonably available means permitted by law and the Disciplinary Rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failing to take adequate action to protect clients' interests before the PTO (e.g., not filing responses, not paying required fees) violates this duty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intentional or habitual violation as aggravating misconduct (Rule 10.89(c)(6))
rubrics_metrics.description: Intentionally or habitually violating the PTO Disciplinary Rules when representing clients before the PTO may constitute a separate disciplinary violation under Rule 10.89(c)(6).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patterns of repeated misconduct across multiple matters can support findings of intentional/habitual violations and more severe discipline, though factual findings on this element must be assessed case-by-case.

rubrics_metrics.name: General practitioner duties to maintain integrity and competence (37 C.F.R. §§ 10.21, 10.76, 10.83)
rubrics_metrics.description: Attorneys who practice before the PTO have a duty to represent their clients competently and zealously and to maintain the integrity and competence of the legal profession.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These overarching duties frame specific disciplinary rules; violations (e.g., abandonment after receiving payment) threaten public protection and the justice system and may warrant exclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Customer number / correspondence address accuracy (37 C.F.R. §§ 1.32(a)(5), 1.76)
rubrics_metrics.description: A customer number contains an applicant's contact information, including the address to which correspondence regarding a patent application should be sent; practitioners must provide correct customer numbers and maintain accurate correspondence addresses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Providing an incorrect customer number or failing to keep address/contact information current can cause PTO communications to be misdelivered, lead to abandonment, and support disciplinary findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors to consider in imposing sanctions (37 C.F.R. § 11.54(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: When determining appropriate sanctions, the Tribunal must consider: (1) whether the practitioner violated a duty owed to a client, the public, the legal system, or the profession; (2) whether the practitioner acted intentionally, knowingly, or negligently; (3) the amount of actual or potential injury caused; and (4) the existence of any aggravating or mitigating factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These four enumerated considerations guide selection of sanctions (e.g., exclusion is supported by intentional abandonment causing actual harm and absence of mitigating factors).

rubrics_metrics.name: Forms of relief available in an initial decision (37 C.F.R. § 11.54(a)(2))
rubrics_metrics.description: An initial decision may contain an order of default judgment, suspension or exclusion from practice, reprimand, or an order dismissing the complaint.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The hearing officer's authority in an initial decision is limited to these forms of relief; other remedies (e.g., restitution) are not listed among forms of relief available in an initial decision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authority regarding restitution (Rule 11.20(b) and Director's powers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rule 11.20(b) authorizes the USPTO Director to require that a practitioner pay restitution as a condition of probation or reinstatement, but the hearing officer issuing an initial decision under Rule 11.54 does not have authority to order restitution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requests for restitution in an initial decision may be denied as beyond the hearing officer's authority; restitution may be imposed later by the Director as a condition of probation/reinstatement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duties of excluded practitioners and reinstatement process (37 C.F.R. §§ 11.58 and 11.60)
rubrics_metrics.description: Excluded practitioners have specified duties under § 11.58, and petitions for reinstatement must comply with § 11.60.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A practitioner subject to exclusion must follow post-exclusion obligations and the formal procedures and standards for any future petition for reinstatement set by the rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication of disciplinary findings
rubrics_metrics.description: Facts and circumstances of disciplinary proceedings shall be fully published in the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office's official publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disciplinary decisions (including exclusions) are public and will be published; publication is a standard consequence and serves public notice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Neglect of client matters as grounds for severe discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: The neglect of client matters is a serious ethical violation that has supported disbarment and exclusion in multiple jurisdictions and in PTO practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Precedent cited shows that abandoning clients after being paid for legal services can result in disbarment or exclusion from practice before the PTO; repeated patterns across many matters are especially aggravating.
